title: Lomi
intro: Thick egg noodles in a hearty, starchy soup with pork, liver, vegetables and ribbons of egg. It is thick enough to coat a spoon, and most people finish it with soy sauce, calamansi and chopped onion at the table.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot and fry the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the pork and cook until lightly browned, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the broth, bring to a boil and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the noodles, kikiam and carrot and simmer until the noodles are soft.
Add the liver, cabbage, soy sauce and fish sauce and cook until the liver is just done.
Stir the cornstarch mixture and pour it in while stirring. Simmer until the soup thickens.
Pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream, stirring gently so they form ribbons. Season with pepper.
Serve topped with chicharon and scallions, with calamansi, chopped onion and soy sauce at the table.

tips: Lomi thickens as it sits. Serve it straight from the pot and thin leftovers with hot broth.

title: Kinalas
intro: Bicolano noodle soup: noodles in a pork broth topped with tender shredded pork, a thick brown sauce, a boiled egg and toasted garlic. Savory and rich, with the gravy slowly melting into the broth as you eat.

items.name: pork hock or bone-in pork shoulder
fresh egg noodles or thick rice noodles

steps.text: Put the pork, water, onion, garlic and peppercorns in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim.
Cover and simmer until the meat falls off the bone.
Lift out the pork and pull the meat and skin into shreds. Strain the broth and season it with the fish sauce.
For the sauce, heat the oil and cook the garlic and onion until soft. Add the 2 cups of broth, soy sauce and sugar and bring to a boil.
Stir in the flour mixture and simmer, stirring, until thick and glossy.
Cook the noodles in boiling water according to the package and drain into bowls.
Ladle hot broth over the noodles, pile on the shredded pork, spoon the sauce on top and finish with egg, scallions and garlic. Serve with calamansi.

tips: Pork head meat is traditional if your butcher sells it cleaned; simmer it the same way until very soft.

title: Odong
intro: Thick, round odong noodles simmered with canned sardines in tomato sauce, patola and malunggay. It is a cheap, filling Visayan and Mindanao favorite with a savory, lightly tangy broth.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the sardines with their sauce, break them into chunks and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Add the odong noodles and simmer, stirring now and then.
Add the patola and simmer until the noodles and patola are both soft.
Taste before seasoning, then add salt or fish sauce and pepper. Stir in the malunggay, turn off the heat and serve.

tips: Odong drinks up the broth quickly, so add a splash of hot water if it gets too thick before serving.

title: Ilocos miki
intro: A thick, golden noodle soup of fresh flat egg noodles and shredded chicken, colored with annatto and finished with ribbons of egg. It is savory, comforting and hearty enough for breakfast.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken in the water with the quartered onion until cooked. Lift out, shred the meat and strain the broth.
Warm the oil and annatto seeds in a pot over low heat until the oil is deep orange. Discard the seeds.
Fry the garlic and minced onion in the annatto oil until soft.
Add the broth, chicken and fish sauce and bring to a boil.
Add the noodles and simmer, stirring, until tender; their starch will thicken the soup.
Stir in the starch mixture and simmer until the soup is thick and glossy.
Drizzle in the eggs while stirring gently. Season with pepper and serve topped with scallions and toasted garlic.

tips: Crushed chicharon on top is a common extra. Eat it right away; the noodles keep softening in the pot.

title: Sinanta
intro: A Cagayan noodle soup with two kinds of noodles, flat egg noodles and rice vermicelli, plus chicken and clams in an annatto-tinted broth. It is savory and briny, with plenty of garlic and scallions.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken in the water with the quartered onion until cooked. Lift out, shred the meat and strain the broth.
Warm the oil and annatto seeds over low heat until the oil is orange, then discard the seeds.
Fry the garlic and sliced onion in the annatto oil until soft.
Add the broth, chicken and fish sauce and bring to a boil.
Add the clams and boil until the shells open. Discard any that stay shut.
Add the egg noodles and simmer until tender.
Add the bihon and cook until heated through. Season with pepper.
Serve topped with scallions and toasted garlic.

tips: Soak the clams in salted water for an hour before cooking so they spit out their sand.

title: Beef pares
intro: Tender beef braised in a sweet soy and star anise sauce, served as a set with garlic fried rice and a bowl of clear beef broth. The sweet, sticky beef and the light, peppery soup balance each other.

steps.text: Put the beef, water, quartered onion and peppercorns in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim, then cover and simmer until the beef is tender.
Ladle 5 cups of the broth into a small pot. Season it with the fish sauce and keep it hot for serving.
Heat the oil in a wide pan. Cook the minced garlic and chopped onion until soft.
Add the beef, soy sauce, sugar, star anise and 1 1/2 cups of the remaining broth. Simmer until the sauce reduces and darkens.
Stir in the cornstarch mixture and simmer until the sauce is glossy.
For the garlic rice, fry the garlic in the oil until golden, add the rice and salt and toss until hot.
Serve each plate of rice and beef with a bowl of the hot broth topped with scallions.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the beef tender in about 40 minutes. Chili garlic oil on the side is the usual extra.

title: Crab and corn soup
intro: A thick, silky soup of creamed corn and crab with soft ribbons of egg white, the kind served at Chinese-Filipino banquets. Sweet from the corn and gently briny from the crab.

steps.text: Melt the butter in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the broth and creamed corn and bring to a boil, then simmer.
Add the crab, fish sauce and white pepper and simmer.
Stir the cornstarch mixture and pour it in while stirring. Simmer until thickened.
Turn the heat to low and pour in the egg whites in a thin stream, stirring slowly so they form ribbons.
Stir in the sesame oil, top with scallions and serve.

tips: Flaked crab sticks work well and are what many home cooks use. Add them at the end so they stay tender.

title: Chicken corn soup
intro: Diced chicken simmered in a creamy corn broth with whole kernels, malunggay and a swirl of egg. It is sweet, mild and filling, an easy soup for kids.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, until no longer pink outside, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then simmer until the chicken is tender.
Add the creamed corn and kernels and simmer, stirring so it does not catch.
Season with the fish sauce and pepper.
Pour in the egg in a thin stream while stirring. Turn off the heat, add the malunggay and serve.

tips: Stir the bottom of the pot often after the creamed corn goes in; it scorches easily.

title: Suam na mais
intro: Fresh corn scraped off the cob and simmered with shrimp and chili leaves or malunggay into a thick, naturally sweet soup. Simple, savory and best with fresh white corn.

items.name: ears of fresh corn
items.note: white glutinous corn or sweet corn

steps.text: Boil the shrimp heads and shells in the water, pressing the heads to release their juices. Strain and keep the liquid.
Meanwhile, grate or scrape the corn kernels off the cobs with a knife, catching the milky juice.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft. Add the corn and stir for 2 minutes.
Pour in the shrimp liquid and bring to a boil, then simmer, stirring often, until the corn is tender and the soup thickens.
Add the shrimp and cook until pink.
Season with the fish sauce and pepper. Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and serve.

tips: Grated corn sticks easily, so keep stirring once it goes in. Thinly sliced pork can be sauteed with the garlic for a meatier version.

title: Nido soup
intro: A delicate, thickened chicken soup with soft strands of bird's nest, shredded chicken, egg white ribbons and quail eggs. It is light and smooth, served at Chinese-Filipino feasts and special dinners.

steps.text: Drain the soaked nido and pick out any small feathers or specks with tweezers.
Poach the chicken breast in the broth with the onion until cooked. Lift out the chicken, shred it finely and discard the onion.
Return the chicken to the broth, add the nido and simmer gently.
Season with the fish sauce and white pepper.
Stir the cornstarch mixture and pour it in while stirring. Simmer until the soup thickens.
Lower the heat and drizzle in the egg whites, stirring slowly so they form ribbons.
Add the quail eggs and sesame oil, top with scallions and serve.

tips: Soak the nido in cold water for 2 to 4 hours, or as the package directs, until it softens and separates into strands. Do this before you start.

title: Hototay soup
intro: A Chinese-Filipino vegetable soup loaded with pork, liver, shrimp, mushrooms, quail eggs and greens in a lightly thickened broth. Savory, colorful and almost a meal on its own.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft. Add the pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add the broth and mushrooms, bring to a boil and simmer.
Add the carrot and simmer.
Add the liver and shrimp and cook until the shrimp turn pink.
Add the cabbage, snow peas and bok choy and cook until just tender. Season with the soy sauce, fish sauce and pepper.
Stir in the cornstarch mixture and simmer until lightly thickened.
Drizzle in the beaten egg while stirring gently. Add the quail eggs and sesame oil and serve.

tips: Some cooks add sliced chicken or squid balls. Keep the vegetables crisp; they continue to soften in the hot soup.

title: Binakol
intro: Chicken simmered in fresh coconut water with ginger and lemongrass, then finished with young coconut strips, green papaya and leafy greens. The broth is clear, gently sweet and fragrant.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the chicken and cook until lightly colored, about 5 minutes. Add the fish sauce and stir.
Pour in the coconut water and water, add the lemongrass and bring to a boil. Skim.
Cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.
Add the papaya and simmer until tender.
Add the coconut meat and heat through. Taste and season with pepper and fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, stir in the leaves and serve.

tips: Use coconut water straight from the fruit, not the sweetened bottled kind, or the soup turns sugary.

title: Tinuom
intro: Ilonggo chicken seasoned with tomatoes, onion, ginger and lemongrass, wrapped in banana leaves and simmered in a pot. Each packet holds its own fragrant, smoky-sweet broth to pour over rice.

items.name: banana leaf squares
items.note: about 30 cm each, wilted over a flame

steps.text: Mix the chicken with the tomatoes, onion, ginger, garlic, lemongrass, salt, fish sauce and pepper. Let it sit while you prepare the leaves.
Lay two banana leaf squares on top of each other, shiny side up. Spoon a quarter of the chicken and its juices into the center.
Add 2 tablespoons of the water, fold the leaves over into a loose packet and tie with kitchen string. Repeat to make 4 packets.
Set the packets in a wide pot and add the remaining water. Cover and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer until the chicken is tender. Add a little water if the pot runs dry.
Serve one packet per person in a bowl and open it at the table so the broth spills out.

tips: Leave room in each packet for the juices to collect, and tie it firmly so the broth stays inside.

title: Linagpang na manok
intro: Grilled chicken pulled into pieces and steeped in a hot lemongrass and ginger broth with raw tomato, onion and chili. The char gives the clear broth a smoky taste that makes this soup distinct.

steps.text: Rub the chicken with the salt and pepper.
Grill over charcoal or in a grill pan over medium heat, turning, until charred in spots and cooked through.
Meanwhile, simmer the water with the lemongrass and ginger.
Cut or pull the grilled chicken into large pieces and add them to the broth. Simmer so the smoke flavors the soup.
Season the broth with the fish sauce.
Divide the tomatoes, onion and chilies among bowls. Ladle in the chicken and boiling broth and let it stand for 2 minutes. Top with scallions.

tips: Native chicken (manok bisaya) is the usual choice if you can get it; simmer it a little longer since it is tougher.

title: Linagpang na isda
intro: Charcoal-grilled fish in a hot lemongrass and ginger broth poured over raw tomatoes, onion and chili. Smoky, fresh and light, with the vegetables just barely wilted.

items.name: medium tilapia or 1 large bangus
items.note: about 800 g in all, scaled and gutted

steps.text: Rub the fish inside and out with the salt.
Grill over medium charcoal or in a grill pan until the skin is charred and the flesh is cooked through, turning once.
Meanwhile, simmer the water with the lemongrass and ginger.
Cut the grilled fish into chunks.
Season the broth with the fish sauce and bring back to a rolling boil.
Divide the tomatoes, onion, chilies and fish among bowls. Ladle the boiling broth over, let it stand for 2 minutes and top with scallions.

tips: Oil the grill and the fish skin well so it does not stick and tear.

title: Pesang manok
intro: Chicken poached in rice washing with ginger and whole peppercorns, with potatoes, napa cabbage and bok choy. The broth is mild and gingery, perfect with a fish sauce and calamansi dip.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger and onion until fragrant.
Add the chicken and cook until lightly colored, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the rice washing, add the peppercorns and bring to a boil. Skim, then cover and simmer.
Add the potatoes and simmer until tender.
Add the napa cabbage and cook until just soft.
Add the bok choy and scallions, season with the fish sauce and turn off the heat. Serve with rice and fish sauce with calamansi.

tips: A sauteed miso and tomato sauce, as served with pesang isda, goes well with this too.

title: Pesang isda
intro: Fish gently poached in rice washing with ginger, peppercorns and napa cabbage, served with a sauteed miso and tomato sauce on the side. The soup is clean and mild; the miso sauce brings the salt and depth.

items.name: fish such as dalag, tilapia or lapu-lapu
items.note: cleaned and cut into thick slices

steps.text: Rub the fish with the salt and set aside.
Heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the ginger and onion until fragrant.
Add the rice washing, peppercorns and potatoes. Bring to a boil and simmer until the potatoes are nearly tender.
Lay in the fish and simmer gently without stirring until it flakes.
Add the napa cabbage and cook until soft, then the bok choy and scallions. Season with the fish sauce.
For the sauce, heat the oil in a small pan and cook the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes break down.
Stir in the miso and water and cook for 2 minutes. Serve the soup with the miso sauce on the side.

tips: Some cooks fry the fish lightly before poaching so it holds together better; either way, swirl the pot instead of stirring.

title: Kinamatisang manok
intro: Chicken simmered in a broth built on plenty of ripe tomatoes, with fish sauce and pechay. The soup is tangy-sweet, savory and bright red, and very good spooned over rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring and pressing, until they collapse into a thick sauce.
Add the chicken and fish sauce and stir for about 5 minutes so the chicken takes on color.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.
Add the chilies and bok choy and cook for 1 minute. Season with pepper and serve.

tips: Use the ripest, softest tomatoes you can find; they give the broth its color and body.

title: Kinamatisang baboy
intro: Pork browned in its own fat, then simmered in a broth of ripe tomatoes and fish sauce with kangkong. Rich, tangy and savory, a soupy ulam for rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the pork and cook, turning, until it browns and renders some fat.
Push the pork aside and cook the garlic and onion in the fat until soft.
Add the tomatoes and fish sauce and cook, pressing the tomatoes, until they break down.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and skim. Cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the kangkong stems first, then the leaves and chili, and cook for 1 minute. Season with pepper and serve.

tips: Pechay or malunggay can stand in for kangkong.

title: Linarang
intro: A Cebuano fish soup of firm fish steaks in a broth of tomatoes, ginger, lemongrass and salty fermented black beans. Savory and a little spicy, with a deep flavor from the beans.

items.name: firm fish steaks such as marlin (malasugi), tuna or mackerel

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pot and cook the garlic, onion and ginger until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until soft.
Stir in the black beans for 1 minute.
Add the water and lemongrass, bring to a boil and simmer so the broth develops.
Lay in the fish and simmer gently, without stirring, until cooked through.
Taste before adding the fish sauce, since the beans are salty. Add the chilies, top with scallions and serve.

tips: Some cooks add a few slices of kamias for a sour edge. Rinse the tausi well or the soup can turn too salty.

title: Sinabawang halaan
intro: Clams cooked open in a quick ginger and tomato broth with pechay. The clam juices make the soup sweet and briny, and it is on the table in about half an hour.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant. Add the tomato and cook until soft.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Add the clams and chili, cover and boil until the shells open.
Discard any clams that stay closed. Taste the broth, then season with fish sauce and pepper.
Add the bok choy, turn off the heat and serve once it wilts.

tips: Soak the clams in salted water for an hour before cooking so they spit out their sand, then lift them out rather than pouring them into a colander.

title: Sinabawang talaba
intro: Shucked oysters poached for a moment in a ginger broth with chayote and malunggay. The oysters stay plump and soft and give the soup a rich, briny sweetness.

steps.text: Pick over the oysters for bits of shell. Strain their liquor through a fine sieve and keep it.
Heat the oil in a pot and fry the ginger, garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the water, oyster liquor and chayote. Bring to a boil and simmer until the chayote is tender.
Add the oysters and cook just until their edges curl.
Season with fish sauce and pepper. Turn off the heat, add the malunggay and serve.

tips: Oysters toughen fast; take the pot off the heat as soon as the edges ruffle.

title: Utan Bisaya
intro: A Visayan vegetable soup of squash, string beans, okra and eggplant simmered in a lemongrass and ginger broth with leafy greens. No sauteing and no meat, just clean, sweet vegetable flavor.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil with the lemongrass, ginger, onion and tomatoes and simmer.
Add the squash and simmer until it starts to soften.
Add the string beans and simmer.
Add the okra and eggplant and simmer until all the vegetables are tender.
Season with the salt and pepper. Add the leaves, cook for 1 minute and serve with rice.

tips: Let a few pieces of squash fall apart into the broth; they thicken it and make it sweeter.

title: Law-oy
intro: A Visayan vegetable soup of squash, patola and malunggay seasoned with dried fish. The fish adds a salty, smoky depth to the light, sweet broth.

items.name: dried fish (bulad), such as danggit or salted dried fish

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the garlic, onion and tomato until soft.
Add the water and dried fish, bring to a boil and simmer to flavor the broth.
Add the squash and simmer until almost tender.
Add the patola and simmer until soft.
Taste before adding salt, since the fish is salty. Stir in the malunggay, turn off the heat and serve.

tips: Corn kernels, okra or string beans are common additions; use whatever vegetables you have.

title: Buridibud
intro: Ilocano vegetable soup where soft sweet potato is mashed into a fermented fish broth to thicken it, then filled with okra, saluyot and malunggay. Earthy, savory and slightly sweet.

steps.text: Bring the water and fermented fish paste to a boil and simmer.
Strain out any bones and solids if your paste is chunky, then return the broth to the pot.
Add the onion, tomato and sweet potato and simmer until the sweet potato is very soft.
Mash about half of the sweet potato against the side of the pot to thicken the broth.
Add the okra and simmer until tender.
Add the saluyot and malunggay, cook for 1 minute, taste and serve.

tips: Flaked grilled fish on top makes it a full meal. Squash can stand in for the sweet potato.

title: Tiyula itum
intro: A Tausug beef soup turned nearly black with a paste of burnt coconut, simmered with ginger, turmeric, lemongrass and chilies. The broth is smoky, nutty and peppery-hot.

steps.text: Toast the grated coconut in a dry wok over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until it turns very dark brown to almost black, about 20 minutes.
Pound the hot coconut in a mortar, or grind it in a food processor, until it becomes a dark, oily paste.
Heat the oil in a large pot and cook the garlic, onion, ginger, turmeric and lemongrass until fragrant.
Add the beef and cook, stirring, until the outside is browned, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and skim. Cover and simmer until the beef is tender.
Stir in the burnt coconut paste, salt and pepper and simmer so the broth darkens and thickens slightly.
Add the chilies, taste for salt and serve topped with scallions, with rice.

tips: Keep the coconut moving while it toasts; it goes from black to bitter and acrid quickly if left alone. Goat meat is also used in place of beef.

title: Etag soup
intro: Cordillera salt-cured pork simmered with ginger until tender, then cooked with chayote and leafy greens. The etag gives the clear broth a deep, salty, slightly funky flavor.

items.name: bunch bok choy or mustard greens

steps.text: Rinse the etag well and soak it in fresh water to draw out some of the salt. Drain.
Put the etag, the 8 cups of water, ginger and onion in a pot and bring to a boil. Skim.
Cover and simmer until the etag is tender.
Add the chayote and simmer until tender.
Taste before adding any salt. Add the greens and pepper, cook for 1 minute and serve.

tips: Etag varies a lot in saltiness; taste the broth after the first 15 minutes and add water if it is too strong. Chicken pieces can be added with the etag for a heartier pot.
